articles.title: DeepSeek and MiniMax clear China AI export controls for overseas use - The Next Web
articles.summary: DeepSeek and MiniMax clear China AI export controls for overseas use  The Next Web
articles.full_text:
“Since the policy was announced, two leading companies, DeepSeek and MiniMax, have successfully completed the registration process and obtained open-source and overseas licensing rights.”
That is what Yuyuan Tantian, a WeChat account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, said in a post late on Thursday. The post sets out how the China AI export controls proposed on 16 October will work. Most AI technology will stay free to export, it said.
DeepSeek and MiniMax did not immediately reply to requests for comment, Reuters reported. DeepSeek reportedly raised $15bn from Tencent and CATL this week. TNW has not independently verified the post.
Data, sensitive uses and computing power
The commerce and science ministries want to add 23 AI technologies to China’s list of technologies banned or restricted from export. They include large models, agents and computing clusters, according to the ministry’s announcement. Companies must register before they export a listed technology. Public comments close on 15 November.
The post said the rules target three areas. The first is data. The rules would ban exports of large models trained on China’s “core data”. They would restrict models trained on “important data”, whatever their size.
The second is sensitive use. Agents above a set performance level face restrictions. Agents built mainly for critical information infrastructure, defence or core government affairs face a ban.
The third is computing power. AI chip design and high-speed links for large computing clusters are on the list.
The catalogue also sets numbers for large models, the post said. They are training compute above 1026 floating-point operations, more than 2 trillion parameters, or capability in the global top ten.
What stays outside the rules
Offering a restricted model through API calls, apps, web pages, SaaS or lightweight local deployment is not a technology export, the post said.
“Simply put, AI companies can continue with their commercialization efforts as usual,” it said.
Open-source technology gets automatic licensing, which the post described as “immediate reporting and export”. So do Chinese companies’ own computing centres abroad, chip tape-out overseas, joint research and work on international standards.
Technology already public through open source or academic papers falls outside the rules. Exports tied to cooperation among members of the World AI Cooperation Organization would get more support.
The lawyers in the room
Liu Jing and Liu Hongmei of Beijing Dacheng Law Offices took part in the consultations, the post said. The control points for some AI items changed after the first draft, they told the account. Many of the concerns companies raised show up in the published version, they said.
Restricted technologies can still go abroad with a licence, Liu Hongmei said. That would not disrupt companies’ overseas plans.
A contrast with Washington
The post set the rules against the US approach. It cited the Commerce Department’s AI diffusion framework of January 2025. It also cited an “alliance strategy” it attributed to Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei.
“But China did not take this path,” the post said.
In a separate post on Friday, the account said overseas internet users had urged other Chinese open-source models to follow suit, Reuters reported.

articles.title: China tightens drone export controls, raising supply chain risks for the US, Europe, and Ukraine - Army Recognition
articles.summary: China tightens drone export controls, raising supply chain risks for the US, Europe, and Ukraine  Army Recognition
articles.full_text:
Breaking News
China tightens drone export controls, raising supply chain risks for the US, Europe, and Ukraine.
China’s Ministry of Commerce, General Administration of Customs, and Central Military Commission Equipment Development Department jointly released Announcement No. 49, establishing revised dual-use export controls on 13 categories of high-performance drone components effective November 18. The decision introduces new licensing mandates for heavy multirotor brushless propulsion systems, high-voltage speed controllers, carbon-fiber propellers, long-range autopilots, and autonomous navigation software while easing registration procedures for standard civilian UAVs.
This regulatory shift aims to exert strategic control over foreign supply chains that feed long-range reconnaissance, cargo, and strike drone manufacturing, without imposing blanket prohibitions on commercial trade. (Picture source: Chinese MoD)
On October 19, 2026, China announced new export controls on 13 categories of drone components, including propulsion, flight control electronics, communications, software, and manufacturing technologies, introducing new restrictions on selected high-performance components and complete drones while easing requirements for certain civilian drones. Announcement No. 49, issued by China's Ministry of Commerce, General Administration of Customs, and Central Military Commission Equipment Development Department, takes effect on November 18. It covers qualifying brushless motors, electronic speed controllers, carbon-fiber propellers, autopilots, and drones with ranges of at least 300 km. The decision comes as Ukraine wants to produce 6 to 7 million small FPV drones in 2026, Russia obtains an estimated 80% of critical drone electronics from Chinese suppliers, and the U.S. seeks more than 200,000 drones by 2027.
Rather than banning exports, Beijing is introducing additional licensing requirements for selected components whose availability could determine whether foreign manufacturers can sustain production of larger reconnaissance, cargo, and long-range military UAVs. The revised classifications distinguish drones according to endurance, range, propulsion, and communications performance. Under 9A012.a, drones capable of controlled flight beyond natural visual range are covered when endurance reaches three hours, or between 30 minutes and three hours if they can take off and maintain stable flight in gusts of at least 46.3 km/h. Classification 9A112.a separately covers drones with ranges of at least 300 km, while the threshold for autonomous or beyond-visual-range aerosol-dispensing UAVs increases fourfold, from more than 20 L to more than 80 L.
Related topic: Taiwan delivers 1,520 FPV attack drones for U.S. Drone Dominance Program to reduce reliance on China
Eligible drones in the 30-minute to less-than-three-hour category can use simplified registration procedures, reducing administrative requirements compared with conventional licensing. However, exporters must declare the characteristics of controlled equipment and products close to regulatory thresholds, with Chinese customs authorized to suspend clearance during classification reviews. Consequently, even shipments ultimately approved for export may face additional verification and delivery delays. Electric propulsion restrictions concentrate on larger multirotors rather than conventional short-range FPV drones. Under 9A901.a, controlled brushless motors must simultaneously operate at a rated voltage of at least 48 V, produce at least 3 kW, achieve at least 3 kW/kg power density, and have a rated speed no greater than 3,000 rpm.
A qualifying 3 kW motor must therefore weigh no more than 1 kg, while a hexacopter using six such motors incorporates 18 kW of aggregate rated power and requires six compatible electronic speed controllers, themselves controlled when rated for at least 48 V and 3 kW. Restrictions also cover selected carbon-fiber propellers, including blades measuring at least 762 mm from rotation center to tip, equivalent to a 60-inch diameter for a symmetric propeller, and specified variable-pitch designs. These components are relevant to cargo UAVs and heavy multirotors because motor torque, electrical power, and propeller dimensions influence payload capacity and endurance. Separate controls cover drone engines exceeding 16 kW, turbojets producing at least 400 N of thrust, and engines designed for operations above 15,420 m.
Chinese manufacturers potentially exposed include Shenzhen Hobbywing Technology, whose high-voltage propulsion products include 50 V and 65 V motor lines, as well as Nanchang Sanrui Intelligence Technology, whose overseas sales reached 524.6 million yuan in 2025. The flight-control provisions address capabilities required for autonomous operations, sustained reconnaissance, and navigation under electronic warfare conditions. Classification 7A103.b covers specially designed UAV autopilots, while 9E901 includes swarm coordination, inertial navigation, terrain matching, interference-resistant satellite navigation, obstacle avoidance, and complete drone design technologies. Autopilots reduce continuous operator intervention, while inertial navigation maintains position estimates without satellite reception but accumulates errors over time; terrain matching can provide an additional reference when suitable geographical information is available.
Communications equipment specially designed for qualifying UAVs is also controlled when airborne radiated power reaches 30 dBm, equivalent to 1 W, or when one station can control more than ten units. The measures also cover unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) technologies meeting five simultaneous criteria, including 75% semantic image compression, image reconstruction within 150 milliseconds, natural-language responses within one second, and 95% task success in unfamiliar environments. Restrictions on these technologies may affect industrial development, as replacing an imported controller does not reproduce the algorithms, integration expertise, or qualification procedures needed for reliable autonomous operations. Ukraine's exposure varies between small FPV quadcopters, heavy-lift multirotors, and longer-range reconnaissance or strike drones.
Ukrainian purchases accounted for an estimated 60% of DJI's global Mavic production in 2023, although this figure does not measure Chinese component content in Ukrainian-made drones today. Conventional 5-inch and 7-inch FPV drones generally fall below the new propulsion thresholds, and their batteries, cameras, and fiber-optic cables are not automatically controlled under 9A901. Larger drones face greater exposure: manufacturing 2,000 qualifying hexacopters requires 12,000 motors and 12,000 compatible controllers, making shortages in either category sufficient to interrupt assembly. Ukraine's projected production of 6 million to 7 million FPV drones in 2026 represents 500,000 to 583,333 units monthly, magnifying the consequences of component shortages and price increases.
Its July 1 defense-export framework allocates 20% of finished-product export proceeds and 30% of component-export proceeds to a state defense fund, but expanding domestic assembly does not eliminate dependence on imported semiconductors, magnets, battery cells, and propulsion systems. Russia's dependence on Chinese electronics could create a separate vulnerability, although existing import figures cannot establish how much production falls under the revised controls. A September 2026 estimate placed Chinese-origin components at 80% of critical electronics used in Russian drones, while China's share of Russian imports of G7-designated common high-priority goods increased from 54.3% in 2022 to 84.6% in 2025. Chinese supplies reached $4.21 billion of the $4.98 billion total, leaving $770 million from other countries and representing a 30.3-percentage-point increase in three years.
Following Ukrainian strikes against Russian fiber-optic production in April 2025, greater reliance on Chinese imports coincided with estimated price increases of 150% by August 2026, although fiber-optic cables are not newly controlled under Announcement No. 49. The directly relevant categories instead include qualifying propulsion equipment, autopilots, navigation technologies, and long-range drones, whose precise shares in Russian manufacturing remain unknown. Beijing's licensing authority nevertheless allows differentiated treatment of exporters, destinations, and end users, creating potential leverage over selected Ukrainian supply chains without requiring a general export prohibition on Russian ones. The U.S. and Europe face substantial cost and production constraints as they attempt to reduce their dependence on Chinese drone components.
In January 2026, the European Parliament estimated that the U.S. and China together supplied 60% of drone components, while Chinese manufacturers accounted for nine out of ten optical or sensor systems used for target identification and engagement. China also controlled an estimated 85% of global lithium battery capacity and 98% of rare-earth refining, affecting battery cells and permanent magnets used in electric motors. EU manufacturers supplied less than 30% of military drones used by member states, while Rabobank estimated that increasing European procurement to 60% would raise European value added to only 51%. In the United States, Chinese brushless motors cost $12–$25 each in November 2025, compared with $100–$225 for American alternatives, although these prices concern smaller motors rather than necessarily those newly controlled.
The Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program initially planned 30,000 drones at roughly $5,000 each, with subsequent purchases targeting $2,300 and more than 200,000 aircraft by 2027. articles.title: ‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far
articles.summary: As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under TrumpWith the midterm elections fast approaching, many Americans have the economy on their minds.US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
US voters are exhausted by years of higher prices. Donald Trump won the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.
In Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”
Economic data paints a different picture. Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.
These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recent Harris poll for the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.
Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.
Inflation
The rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.
In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.
That’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.
The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.
It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.
Gas prices
In the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll, gas prices were the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.
Soon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.
Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.
Monthly job figures
The labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.
Employers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.
S&P 500
Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.
Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.
While many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, who own nearly half of the stock market investments.
Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to a K-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.
Interest rates
Interest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.
For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.
When Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.
Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.
For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fed hiked rates for the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.
Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.

articles.title: Should we tip on takeout? We weighed all angles and the answer is …
articles.summary: Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal normYou arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.What’s the right thing to do? Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
You arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.
What’s the right thing to do?
Start with the situations where our instincts are clearest. Tipping is normal at restaurants, in taxis or after haircuts. We don’t usually tip when we buy fast food, ride on a bus or have the plumbing fixed.
What explains the difference? One way to think about it is through economics. A server’s pay, in effect, is split in two: a salary paid by the restaurant, and a tip paid directly by you, the customer. But why do you get a say in the server’s pay when you don’t have that role in other cases?
The logic is simple: you’re in a better position than the restaurant owner to judge the quality of the service.
You know whether the server was fast or slow – so your tip rates it as baseline, above baseline or below baseline. A low tip, though, can feel confrontational: you’re delivering your verdict in front of the person you’re judging.
And it’s not just restaurants. A cab company knows how far the driver went, but not how well the car was driven. You know that, so you leave a tip. The owner of a hair salon knows how many customers were served, but not whether they were served well. Or take housekeepers at a hotel: you don’t watch them work, but you still know something the hotel doesn’t know: how big a mess you left behind.
The common thread is that you know something the employer doesn’t. And that gives you a role in deciding how much the worker gets paid.
But what about the places where we don’t tip?
You don’t tip the cashiers at a fast-food restaurant. Why? The company trains the staff to say the same things every time, then watches them. You don’t see much that the company doesn’t. And the cashier works behind a counter where the pressure to keep moving is already strong.
When you ride the crosstown bus, you don’t usually see anything important the bus company doesn’t, and the prospect of being tipped probably wouldn’t change what the driver does. So you don’t tip.
Or a company sends you a plumber. You might know whether the problem got fixed, but not whether the plumber worked efficiently or cut corners. Since you don’t know anything the boss doesn’t, there’s no reason to give you a direct role in setting the agent’s pay.
Compare this with a case where the plumber has to climb long stairs to reach you or face off against a scary dog. Here, you do know about hidden hardships – hidden from the plumber’s boss, that is – so tipping is a sensible economic gesture as well as a kind one.
Still, the theory only gets us so far. Why don’t people usually tip employees of airlines, front-desk workers at hotels or baggers at the grocery store?
Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place. In some cultures, there’s little or no tipping, and a tip might even be considered an insult.
In fact, our theory above was a better fit in the United States 20 years ago than it is today, because invitations to tip have become more common in places where customers know little that management doesn’t already know.
So why is the pizza place asking you for a tip in the first place?
Some people imagine that the business is trying to get out of paying its clerks what it should; it’s foisting that job on to its customers. But that’s probably the wrong way to look at it. Clerks decide whether to take jobs and keep them based on the total pay they take home, wherever it comes from. Adding tips to their pay, in the long run, will probably hold down the base salaries that they’re paid.
Look at it this way: if all tipping were banned tomorrow, you’d expect the base pay of servers to go up soon afterwards, along with prices on the menu. Otherwise the loss of tips would just be a pay cut; and if restaurants could pay less to their servers without losing them, they’d presumably (alas?) be doing it already.
More likely, the takeout place just needs to somehow raise its prices. They think you’ll react better to an invitation to tip than you would to a more expensive menu, though it comes to the same thing. You’ll use the menu to decide what to buy and won’t think about the tip. Then when tipping is invited at the end, you won’t tell yourself the cafe raised its prices. You’ll just think the culture is changing: everyone wants a tip nowadays! But in effect, the invitation to tip is just a price hike that the owner is hoping you won’t view that way.
There’s another oddity: the timing of the request. An unfamiliar invitation to tip sometimes comes early, when some of the work you’re buying hasn’t been done yet. This might give the server a chance to see your tip before performing and then retaliate on the spot with sluggish service if you seem ungenerous, or do a good job if you’ve been nice.
This order of operations isn’t very consistent with the idea that you’re tipping in order to rate the quality of the work done.
So what should you do when the screen asks you to tip?
In those new settings – bakeries, coffee shop, fast-food places – your choice can function as a kind of vote – not on the quality of service, but on tipping itself. Leaving a tip accepts the invitation to help set the pay and encourages the arrangement to continue. If you don’t tip, you’re saying that you’re against using tips as a way to divide decisions about pay in this situation.
But once tipping is customary – not auditioning for acceptance, but entrenched – then you should tip, at least usually. The obligation isn’t set by law, but you consent to it when you eat at the restaurant. The owner is saying, in effect: your obligation to pay for this meal will be a combination of laws (that make you pay the check) and norms (that make you pay the tip).
You should play by the rules that the business has set or not play at all, even if the rules might seem to defy your theory, or any theory, of when tipping serves a good purpose. But when deciding what to order or where to eat, just remember: 20% of the cost (or whatever the customary tip might be) isn’t shown on the menu.
To put this more generally: if you run into a norm that you aren’t sure you like, ask whether you’re in a position to help shape it or whether you can only decide whether to go along with it.
The bottom line: tipping for takeout doesn’t make sense as a custom. It should be resisted unless it’s entrenched, at which point it’s best viewed as part of the bargain.
Put differently, we would vote against the idea; but having lost the vote, we go along with it.
- Ward Farnsworth is a professor at the University of Texas school of law, and Saul Levmore at the University of Chicago law school. This is an edited excerpt from their new book, Should You Tip for Takeout? Solving the Puzzles of Everyday Life, out now

articles.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
articles.summary: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran  European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.
Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.
The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.
Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.
Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.
It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.
Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.
European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.
